title: Jonah and the Confession
premise: Silas Voss, a retired detective turned failing bookseller, is hired by a frightened woman named Mara Quill who pays in advance to prove that a murder has not yet happened — the predicted killing of a local archivist named Jonah Reyes. As Silas investigates, she uncovers a thirty-year-old case she herself helped close wrongly, one in which an innocent man was convicted on her testimony. The 'prediction' turns out to be a carefully staged confession-by-proxy: Jonah, dying of illness, orchestrated events to force Silas to reopen the old case and expose the true killer — her former partner, now a respected judge. In the end Silas must choose between protecting the last shreds of her loyalty to her old friend and telling the truth that will destroy them both; she testifies, the judge is arrested, and Jonah dies at peace with his name cleared.
about_author: Isandro Pemberton is the pen name of a former court stenographer who spent two decades transcribing testimony before turning to fiction. They write slow-burn mysteries about people haunted by paperwork, and live quietly near a coastal town much like the one in this book.

chapters.title: Paid in Advance
chapters.summary: Third-person limited, Silas. A nervous woman named Mara Quill enters Voss Books at closing time and pays triple to hire Silas for an impossible job: prove that Jonah Reyes will not be murdered next week. Silas, broke and bored, takes the money despite her instincts. The beat is wary curiosity — the hook of an impossible commission.

chapters.title: The Man Who Waits
chapters.summary: Silas's POV. She finds Jonah Reyes, the supposed future victim, alive, calm, and strangely unsurprised by her questions. He works in the county archive and seems to know more about her past than he should. Emotional beat: unease — the victim acts like a man expecting her.

chapters.title: Thirty Years of Dust
chapters.summary: Silas's POV with flashback texture. Researching Jonah leads her to the 1994 Halloway murder case — the conviction that made her career, built partly on her identification of a young dockworker, Elias Brandt. Beat: dread as she realizes Jonah's file sits directly beside Brandt's.

chapters.title: Mara's Alibi
chapters.summary: Alternating Silas and Mara POVs. Mara admits she's Jonah's niece and claims he received an anonymous letter predicting his death, signed with a date only someone from the old case would know. Beat: sympathy curdling into suspicion — is Mara the threat or another pawn?

chapters.title: The Judge's Garden Party
chapters.summary: Silas's POV. She attends a civic event where retired Judge Alden Crane — her old partner — holds court among admirers. Their warm reunion carries an undercurrent she can't name. Beat: nostalgia laced with the first hairline crack of doubt.

chapters.title: A Break-In by the Book
chapters.summary: Silas's POV. Her bookshop is ransacked; only her old case notes are taken. The police are polite and useless. Beat: violation and resolve — someone wants the past to stay buried, which means it's worth digging up.

chapters.title: Elias Brandt's Letters
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. She shares letters Jonah inherited from Brandt, written from prison, insisting a third man was present at the Halloway scene. Beat: grief and growing belief that an innocent man died behind bars.

chapters.title: The Date That Hasn't Happened
chapters.summary: Silas's POV. The letter's predicted date is three days away, and it matches the anniversary of Halloway's death exactly. Silas stakes out Jonah's apartment through a long, silent night. Beat: mounting tension as nothing happens — until she finds the archive door open.

chapters.title: What the Archive Keeps
chapters.summary: Silas's POV. Inside, Jonah shows her evidence he's assembled for decades: a suppressed forensic report naming a second set of prints at Halloway. He asks her not who will kill him, but who killed Halloway. Beat: vertigo — the mystery inverts.

chapters.title: Crane's Kindness
chapters.summary: Silas's POV, intimate and uneasy. Crane offers her financial help for the bookshop, gently probing about her 'new client.' His generosity feels like a leash. Beat: love against duty — her loyalty to him begins to feel like complicity.

chapters.title: The Witness Who Recanted
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. Tracking down a second witness from 1994, they find a dying woman ready to recant her testimony — then find her dead hours later, ruled natural causes. Beat: horror; the past is actively defending itself.

chapters.title: Confession by Proxy
chapters.summary: Silas's POV. Jonah finally explains: he is terminally ill, and the 'predicted murder' was his own construction — bait designed to drag Silas, the only honest witness left, back into the case. Beat: betrayal and reluctant respect.

chapters.title: Threats in First Editions
chapters.summary: Silas's POV. A rare first edition arrives at the shop with a note inside: stop, or Mara pays the price. The killer knows everything. Beat: fear sharpening into protectiveness — Silas now fights for someone, not just something.

chapters.title: Hiding Mara
chapters.summary: Dual POV. Silas hides Mara at a coastal cabin while following the paper trail of the suppressed report — which passed through Crane's chambers in 1995. Beat: quiet intimacy between Silas and Mara, and the first open acknowledgment that Crane may be guilty.

chapters.title: The Partner I Knew
chapters.summary: Silas's POV, reflective centerpiece chapter. A long memory chapter reconstructing her years with Crane: the cases, the trust, the night he covered for her early mistake. Beat: mourning a friendship while it still stands.

chapters.title: Nineteen Ninety-Four, Reopened
chapters.summary: Silas and Jonah's POV. Together they rebuild the Halloway night: Crane was there, the prints were his, and the department buried it to protect a rising star. Beat: cold clarity — the truth assembled piece by piece.

chapters.title: Confrontation at the Courthouse
chapters.summary: Silas's POV. She confronts Crane privately. He neither denies nor confesses; instead he reminds her what testifying will cost her — her reputation, her pension, her name. Beat: the book's moral crux, loyalty versus truth laid bare.

chapters.title: The Date Arrives
chapters.summary: Multi-POV. On the predicted date, someone torches the archive wing; Jonah is hospitalized after going back for the original report. Beat: climax begins — the killer is erasing the last physical evidence.

chapters.title: Smoke and Ashes
chapters.summary: Silas's POV. At Jonah's bedside, he gives her the one thing fire can't take: his sworn statement and a hidden duplicate page. Crane visits the hospital, and Silas watches him lie beautifully to a dying man. Beat: grief transmuted into certainty.

chapters.title: Testimony
chapters.summary: Silas's POV. She files to reopen the case and takes the stand, dismantling her own 1994 identification in open court and naming Crane. Beat: catharsis and self-destruction braided together — she wins the truth and loses her past.

chapters.title: Arrest at Dusk
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. Crane is arrested outside his home; he looks at Silas once across the street and says nothing. Jonah, discharged, watches from a wheelchair. Beat: justice arriving without triumph — quiet, heavy, final.

chapters.title: Jonah and the Confession
chapters.summary: Silas's POV, closing. Jonah dies in early spring, his name cleared, thanking Silas for choosing truth over loyalty. She reopens the bookshop with a new shelf: books about wrongful convictions. Beat: resolution and renewal — identity rebuilt around honesty rather than the badge.
